stories.headline: Alibaba ships Qwen4-Max: 2.4 trillion parameters, 71 billion active, a million-token context and a claimed 60% cut in task cost
stories.why_read: It is the top story on Hacker News this morning and the biggest Chinese model drop since Qwen3.8, with open-weight smaller Qwen4 models promised next.
body: Alibaba made Qwen4-Max generally available on Monday after a preview that began November 11. It is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 2.4 trillion total parameters that activates about 71 billion per token, roughly 25% fewer active parameters than Qwen3.8-Max at the same scale. It reads images and video natively, supports a context of up to one million tokens, and speaks both OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs, with tool calling and structured outputs. Alibaba says it ranked 6th on Code Arena and uses 35% fewer tokens than its predecessor on its own Work360 benchmark, cutting average cost per task by about 60%. Cached input starts at $0.075 per million tokens.

The flagship stays closed, but Alibaba says smaller Qwen4 models will be released as open weights, which is the part LocalLLaMA folks will care about. Coverage notes the benchmark claims, including beating GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 on some coding tests, are Alibaba's own and not independently verified. On Hacker News, one commenter pointed to an Artificial Analysis score of 43 at an average cost of $3.27, against 46 at $0.36 for GPT-6.1 Sol at medium effort, and others hoped the new model is faster to serve than the famously slow Qwen 3.8.

stories.headline: Musk: Starship V4 grows to about 70 meters with nine engines and more than 60% more propellant, as SpaceX eyes 50+ Tbps of Starlink per flight
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this the night after the catch, and it is the natural next chapter: the ship that just came home is about to get a lot bigger.
body: Elon Musk posted that Starship V4 will be about 70 meters long, roughly a 40% length increase, allowing more than 60% more propellant. The engine count rises to nine by adding three more Raptor Vacuum engines, and they will be higher-thrust V4 engines. The post, quoting a picture of Starship's scale, passed 2.3 million views overnight.

A companion post you saved from Nic Cruz Patane says Musk expects future Starship missions to deploy more than 50 Tbps of Starlink capacity per flight, almost double what Starship carries now and roughly 20 times what a Falcon 9 delivers with V2 Mini satellites. Put those together with this weekend's tower catch and the plan is clear: a bigger, reusable upper stage whose main job is to pour bandwidth into orbit.

stories.headline: The router behind Friday's nationwide US ground stop was reportedly a brand-new Juniper unit, not the 2001-era gear first blamed
stories.why_read: As a network-minded architect who reposted both sides of this, it is a perfect incident-review puzzle: was it old routers, or a new box with a chatty feature?
body: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the routers having issues during Friday's outage were bought in 2001, became obsolete in 2006 and were still in use in 2026. Network engineer John Breth quipped that Cisco 6500 and 2950 switches went end of life in 2006, adding that those 6500s were beasts. A later update from International Cyber Digest, which you reposted, tells a different story: the router behind the nationwide ground stop was a brand-new Juniper unit at a remote FAA radio site in Arkansas, just installed by defense contractor L3Harris.

According to that report, FAA officials believe a feature that broadcast data more widely than needed flooded the network. If it holds up, the lesson is less about aging hardware and more about change management: a fresh install with the wrong defaults can take down a system that old gear had kept running for two decades. Expect a formal post-incident report to settle which version is right.

stories.headline: Steve Blank on Nvidia after Jensen Huang: visionary founders are rarely replaced by visionaries, and the board must pick an innovator, not an operator
stories.why_read: After last week's Huang resignation news, this is the most useful long read on what actually happens next, from someone who has watched Silicon Valley succession for decades.
body: Steve Blank argues that Huang reinvented Nvidia three times: CUDA in 2006, funded for years before revenue; the pivot to deep learning after ImageNet in 2012; and the 2020 Mellanox deal that turned Nvidia from a board vendor into a systems company selling integrated AI racks. Each was a business model change, not just a product change, and Blank doubts an execution-focused CEO would have funded CUDA through those lean years.

He compares Microsoft's Ballmer era, when sales tripled to $78 billion while the company missed search, smartphones, media and cloud, with Nadella's turnaround. Nvidia is the extreme case, he writes: Huang had about 60 direct reports, discouraged one-on-ones, kept no long-term plans and did not believe in succession planning. Blank's advice to the board is to look for a product and engineering visionary, not simply the operator next in line. The Hacker News thread passed 380 comments.

stories.headline: Old Bitly links in 2011 tweets from Burger King, McDonald's and Trump were re-registered and pointed at new pages; Bitly confirms the flaw
stories.why_read: Every wiki, runbook and slide deck you own probably has a few short links in it, and this is a sharp reminder that a link is only as permanent as the service behind it.
body: Ransomnews found that a Bitly link in a Burger King tweet from July 2011 had been registered again on November 15 and pointed at Wikipedia's list of Nazi concentration camps; 18 minutes earlier, a link in a 2011 McDonald's tweet was redirected to the article on the September 11 attacks. Neither account was hacked. Checking 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump's tweets from 2009 to 2013, the site found that 56 had been created after the tweets, and CNN later reported redirected links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, the FBI and the Department of Defense.

Bitly confirmed an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links, suspended the accounts involved and began disabling the affected links. By the evening the Burger King and McDonald's links showed Bitly's Link Deactivated page, though 49 re-created Trump links that look like the originals still worked at the last check. If your organization relies on short links in documentation, it is a good week to audit them.

stories.headline: A one-click universal XSS in uBlock Origin's element picker, found mostly by GPT-5.6 Sol, let a malicious site inject scripts into any other site
stories.why_read: It is a clean example of AI-assisted bug hunting on software almost everyone trusts, and the fix is already out, so it is a satisfying read rather than a scary one.
body: Smitty van Bodegom describes a flaw in the Firefox MV2 version of uBlock Origin, with a smaller related issue in uBO Lite, where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript, so an attacker could run code in the context of any site. The trick was to embed the element picker's internal page in an invisible iframe, drive it to the filter the attacker wanted, and position it so the user clicks the hidden Create button.

The hard part on Firefox was learning the extension's random per-install UUID, which the author extracted by hooking a request made by one of uBO's default filter rules. He credits GPT-5.6 Sol with doing most of the work of finding the bug, which he then verified, and says Claude wrote most of the proof-of-concept code. The issue is fixed, and a GitHub advisory has more detail.

stories.headline: A Microsoft 365 outage swallowed a pool system's alarm emails, and 15 hotel guests were hurt by excess chlorine at Phantasialand
stories.why_read: The Hacker News crowd turned this into a masterclass on safety design: never let a life-safety alarm depend on a single cloud email path.
body: German broadcaster WDR reports that during Friday's Microsoft outage, which knocked out Outlook, the Phantasialand theme park in Brühl did not receive emails. Its maintenance safety system had already sent an alarm by email because the automatic dosing system was pumping too much chlorine into the pool at the Hotel Ling Bao. Thirteen guests complained of respiratory irritation, the count rose to 15, four went to hospital and one stayed for observation with a moderate injury. Firefighters found a defect in the dosing system, and the water was replaced.

The top comment on Hacker News, from someone who runs a closed-loop chlorination system, explains that these systems tend to fail by reading low and then overdosing, so a human or an independent sensor must always guard against both extremes. Others put it more bluntly: the outage was Microsoft's, but relying on email alone for a dangerous alarm was the real failure.

stories.headline: Gwynne Shotwell: Grok Bot's paid weekly users more than doubled to 800,000 in about a month
stories.why_read: You run a fleet of these bots yourself, so here is the scale you are part of, and the cost tension that explains the recent usage-limit changes.
body: SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said on the third-quarter earnings call that Grok Bot's paid weekly users more than doubled to 800,000 in about a month, according to a summary of posts on X, and Elon Musk called it the fastest growth of any product he has seen. Users are sharing bots that scan X posts, draft content, run research and act as personal assistants, along with one that builds interactive courses.

The same summary notes executives saying heavy usage costs are rising faster than revenue. That matches another thread on X this weekend in which users describe stretching weekly limits with specialized bots, such as a batcher that queues jobs or a team with courier and librarian roles. Growth plus tighter allowances is the story to watch for anyone running dozens of agents.

stories.headline: The catch did not win the Moon race, it put SpaceX in it: each Starship landing needs about ten refill launches
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this sober take, and it is the right counterweight to a weekend of celebration: reuse is the precondition, not the finish line.
body: A post you saved lays out the math. NASA still has not picked whose lander returns its astronauts to the Moon in 2028 and will take whichever is ready first, Starship or Blue Origin's. Starship cannot reach the Moon on one tank, so roughly ten more Starships have to launch first and refill it in orbit.

Ten launches for every landing only works if ships come home and fly again, and until Saturday no Starship had. Meanwhile, the post notes, China plans two rockets, a lander and astronauts on the Moon before 2030. Orbital refueling is the next big milestone to watch.

stories.headline: One missing tile, orange stains and Musk on a lift: the first close looks at a Starship that came back from orbit
stories.why_read: Three of your bookmarks were about the heat shield, which is the right obsession: rapid reuse lives or dies on those tiles.
body: Everyday Astronaut shared a photo of what one missing tile looks like on the recovered ship, calling it impressive that the rest held up so well, and asked who else wants to see this ship re-fly even if it makes no sense to do so. Another post you saved from Serious Callers Only showed Elon Musk on a lift inspecting the nose tiles.

A third post asked why Starship tiles still get an orange stain when the Space Shuttle's did not, calling the Shuttle the best worst spacecraft ever. Together they make a nice before-and-after for anyone who followed years of tile-loss worries: the first look at a caught orbital ship shows wear, not failure.

stories.headline: Paul Graham, Musk and Garrett Reisman push back on the claim that anyone with SpaceX's money could have caught a Starship
stories.why_read: You reposted three angles on this argument, and Paul Graham's one-liner is the one people will quote all week.
body: Finance writer Matt Stoller argued that SpaceX's wins come down to capital and engineering anyone could buy, and Musk replied by pointing to SpaceX's share of global payload to orbit and the tower catch, according to a summary of posts on X. Paul Graham's response passed a million views: you solve really hard problems for decades and get told anyone could have done it, but as an investor, he says, the limiting factor is not investment, it is founder ability.

Former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman, who spent seven years at SpaceX, added in a clip you reposted that he has met many super smart people who are usually smart about one thing, while Musk moves from software to welding detail with his engineers. John LeFevre's line was the funniest: the engineers who caught the rocket do not write LinkedIn thought pieces about leadership.

stories.headline: Ari Paul: 'I was wrong on SpaceX' and Musk's vertical integration of bottlenecks is the best moat he has seen
stories.why_read: A skeptic changing his mind in public is rare, and his question about which moats survive AI is a good one for any architect thinking about build versus buy.
body: Investor Ari Paul wrote that he had mocked SpaceX's IPO valuation as absurd, but now thinks Musk has been smartly verticalizing and building strategic moats; he does not own shares yet but expects to buy and could see it becoming a large core holding. His argument: if advanced AI lets leading software companies take over many industries, hardware is harder to copy in the short term because factories and supply chains take years, though robotics may close that gap within about five years.

His answer to what remains defensible is Musk's vertical integration of key bottlenecks. The biggest risk, he says, is Musk himself, comparing SpaceX's dependence on him to Nvidia's on Jensen Huang, which reads differently after last week's news.

stories.headline: Ethan Mollick asked Fable and Opus to find the Starship catch video and rebuild its last 40 seconds in 3D with three.js, and they did
stories.why_read: You reposted it, and it is the most fun demo of the weekend: a single prompt turned a webcast into an interactive model with cutaway views.
body: Ethan Mollick shared another thing that would have seemed impossible a few months ago. His prompt asked Claude Fable and Opus to find video of the Starship catch, render the last 40 seconds or so in 3D with three.js in extreme detail, let him switch between views like cutaway blueprints, and skip the crowd. The result is a playable scene with the tower arms and the cloud deck.

When he asked for sources, Claude said the recreation was built from SpaceX's official webcast replay of Flight 15, with a specific window of the video driving the timing, camera shots and catch moment. It is a neat pairing with this weekend's posts about coding agents doing work that is not really code.

stories.headline: @mattyp and Lauren Tan: coding agents are underrated for work that isn't code
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this clip, and it fits how you already use your bot fleet: long, multi-step jobs where planning and clean context matter more than code.
body: In a livestream between @mattyp and Lauren Tan, highlighted by Attia, the point was that coding agents are great at long, complex tasks because they plan, split the work and keep context clean. People are even editing video with them now, and the post asks for the weirdest non-coding job readers have given a coding agent.

It lands at a good time, alongside Tan's team talk about shipping 11,000 pull requests in a month and Mollick's three.js Starship demo. The common thread is that the agent harness, not the programming language, is the valuable part.

stories.headline: Eric S. Raymond, of all people, defends Rust: annoying, yes, but he is shipping a significant amount of it
stories.why_read: You reposted the man who wrote The Cathedral and the Bazaar taking Rust's side, with LLMs as the reason the borrow checker stopped bothering him.
body: Responding to a post that said Rust might be the official language of products that do not actually ship, Eric S. Raymond wrote that he could not believe he had to defend Rust. He lists his gripes, including lifetime tracking, which he calls a huge pain and says he never learned to do by hand before LLMs made it unnecessary, slow compiles and obnoxious evangelists.

None of that, he argues, means the tool lacks uses, and he says he is shipping a significant amount of Rust these days. It is a small but telling data point: AI assistance is lowering the learning curve of strict languages, which may matter more for Rust adoption than any advocacy.

stories.headline: SpaceXAI makes invisible text watermarking in Grok models off by default, days after turning it on for the EU AI Act
stories.why_read: If you build on the Grok API, this changes a default under your feet, and admins now control it per model.
body: SpaceXAI enabled watermarking on November 7 for seven Grok models to meet Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which requires machine-readable marks on AI output, according to a summary of posts on X. Days later it reversed the default to off, letting team admins enable it per model or where the law requires it. Musk said the change prioritizes user control.

Image and video watermarks from Grok Imagine stay visible and mandatory. Reactions split between developers glad to avoid invisible tracking in their text and people questioning how this squares with EU rules.

stories.headline: At CoRL 2026 in Austin, Nvidia shows GR00T 2, an open robot model that learns manipulation from human demos
stories.why_read: It is happening in your town, and it pairs open models with robots, two of your favorite beats.
body: At the Conference on Robot Learning in Austin, Nvidia introduced GR00T 2, an open model that learns manipulation from human demonstrations and transfers skills across robot types, according to a summary of posts on X. The reported success rates are 71% on tasks with a single demonstration and 95% with five.

PrismaX also unveiled a Robotics Data Catalog with camera views, task details, quality scores and downloadable episodes, including work with UPenn's GRASP Lab. The theme of the week is that better data and adaptable models, not just bigger ones, are what move robots into homes and factories.

stories.headline: Asked which public benchmark they trust for frontier models, 56 AI experts picked Terminal-Bench 4
stories.why_read: When everyone claims a win on some leaderboard, as Qwen4-Max does today, it helps to know which evals practitioners actually believe.
body: Chris Barber surveyed 56 AI practitioners about which public benchmarks they trust, excluding any tied to their own work, according to a summary of posts on X. Terminal-Bench 4 led with 25 votes, Terminal-Bench Science followed with 20, and coding tests FrontierCode with 13 and FrontierSWE with 10 rounded out the top.

Respondents liked terminal-based evals because they look like real work in software and science, but many were skeptical that any benchmark captures true progress. That is worth remembering when reading Alibaba's claim that Qwen4-Max is 49% more token efficient on Terminal-Bench 4.0 than its predecessor.

stories.headline: The Xena Project explains what 'the proof is checked in Lean' really proves, especially when an AI wrote the code
stories.why_read: This is the math corner of your pinned post meeting AI head-on, and a clear guide to the trust questions that apply to any verified system.
body: The Xena Project blog walks through how to interpret claims that a theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean. The short version: there is a real signal, but if the Lean code is AI-generated you need to run some tests first. The prompt was OpenAI's recent dump of 722 mathematics papers, about 45% with Lean code, three of which, all without Lean, have been retracted over a sign error.

The key distinction is between a theorem's statement and its proof. The post shows a statement that looks like Fermat's Last Theorem but is trivially false because Lean's natural numbers include zero, and Lean will happily compile the statement itself. It lays out four questions to ask of any repository before trusting its headline theorem, and notes many papers in the OpenAI dump have not yet been checked this way.

stories.headline: Crows process and respond to visual cues about twice as fast as humans and monkeys, a new Science study finds
stories.why_read: A delightful science story to end the weekend on, and a final blow to 'birdbrain' as an insult.
body: The New York Times reports on a study in Science in which two carrion crows, Lemmy and Iggy, veterans of earlier lab work on tool use and counting, processed and responded to visual cues at about twice the speed of humans and monkeys. It is the first time the neural speed of avian decision-making has been quantified.

Neuroscientist Mike Colombo of the University of Otago, who was not involved, said birds are just incredibly fast. The piece traces how scientists long dismissed small bird brains, while recent work shows pigeons telling cancerous cells from healthy ones and corvids recognizing themselves and planning for the future.

stories.headline: Indeed postings are down 46.7% since April 2022, AI is blamed for 121,401 cuts this year, and CS enrollment is falling
stories.why_read: You reposted the hiring numbers, and together these three data points sketch the job market your teams are hiring into.
body: The Kobeissi Letter, in a post you saved, says new Indeed job postings fell 4.8% year over year in the week ending October 16 and are down 46.7% since April 2022, leaving vacancies 0.8% below February 2020 levels. The decline has slowed, but there is no sign of a rebound. A summary of posts on X adds that US employers blamed AI for 121,401 job cuts through October, about 20% of announcements, even as unemployment stays near 4.1% and AI skills command a pay premium.

A separate thread notes US undergraduate computer science enrollment fell more than 12% this fall and graduate enrollment about 10%, according to National Student Clearinghouse data, after an 18.4% undergraduate drop over two years. The usual explanation is AI automating entry-level work and cooling demand for junior roles.

stories.headline: Tor rushes out 0.4.9.17 with IPv6 DoS defenses as a sustained DDoS floods relays across the network
stories.why_read: A real-world case study in defending a decentralized network under attack, with a plea to every relay operator to upgrade now.
body: The Tor Project released 0.4.9.17 with a series of security fixes, including an especially important one for relay DoS defenses related to IPv6 handling. The release is a rapid response to an ongoing DDoS attack that has affected most relay operators, with relays overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits.

The team says this is not an easy problem, it is evaluating more defenses and expects further releases soon. Operators are asked to upgrade as soon as possible, with no other action needed. The announcement closes by thanking everyone except the attackers.

stories.headline: Protomaps makes self-hosting map tiles cheap: the whole 139 GB world map on a CDN for about $5 a month
stories.why_read: A practical homelab and architecture read: one file, HTTP range requests and no per-load API bill.
body: Bruce Röttgers explains PMTiles, the Protomaps tile format that ships as a single file read through HTTP range requests, so it can sit in a storage bucket behind any CDN that caches ranges. For Cloudflare and similar, a small edge function maps classic x/y/z tile URLs to ranges. The CLI can cut out a bounding box or zoom levels for much smaller files.

On Bunny.net, he estimates storing the 139 GB world map with fivefold replication costs about $5 a month, and loading a map of Europe and zooming into a city moves about 5 MB. At roughly $0.05 per thousand loads, that could be 100 times cheaper than Mapbox's $5 per thousand after its free tier.

stories.headline: ParadeDB makes search across normalized Postgres tables up to 1000x faster, so you may not need to denormalize into Elasticsearch
stories.why_read: If you have ever built a fragile ETL just to make search fast, this is the architecture argument for keeping one database.
body: ParadeDB's Stu Hood describes search joins: relevance-ranked queries that span several normalized tables, like users, posts and comments. Teams usually either denormalize into Elasticsearch through an ETL pipeline or accept Postgres slowly scoring and joining millions of rows to return a handful of results.

Using DataFusion, rank joins, co-partitioning and tuple tagging, ParadeDB says a multi-table search over a StackOverflow dataset of 2.3 million users, 20 million posts and 29 million comments dropped from 2 minutes to 100 ms, up to 1000x faster than vanilla Postgres, without extra infrastructure.

stories.headline: It's always DNS, so why is S2 running its own? Route53's update rate limits forced the call
stories.why_read: An honest architecture story about a decision nobody wants to make, with a post-incident review as the turning point.
body: S2 wanted customers to create unlimited basins, each with its own subdomain CNAME that must resolve instantly, so clients are not stuck on a cached NXDOMAIN. Route53 can store unlimited records, but its API was limited to about five upserts per second, which the team learned the hard way when someone rapidly created tens of thousands of basins and DNS updates backed up for hours.

Batching would have broken the instant-availability goal, and other managed DNS providers had similar limits, so the team ended up building and running its own authoritative DNS server. The post is candid about how reluctant they were, which makes it a useful read for anyone weighing the same trade-off.

stories.headline: Cornell's EchoMotion tracks your whole body with sonar from an ordinary smartwatch's speaker and microphone
stories.why_read: Physics plus a tiny AI model on your wrist: no camera, better privacy, and a good reminder that small models matter too.
body: Cornell's SciFi Lab built EchoMotion, which uses the built-in speaker and microphone of a commercial smartwatch as a sonar-like system, with a lightweight AI model, to estimate the position of a person's entire body. Existing wearables mostly track the device itself with accelerometers and gyroscopes, so full-body tracking has needed phones, earbuds, headsets or cameras.

Acoustic sensing protects the privacy of the wearer and those nearby and produces less data to process, which also saves battery. The team presented the work at UbiComp in Shanghai and sees uses in workouts, daily activity tracking and physical rehabilitation.

stories.headline: 'All AI-generated code should be open source': a hot take that drew more than 1,100 points on Hacker News
stories.why_read: Agree or not, it is the licensing debate your legal team will eventually ask about, and the thread is unusually substantive.
body: Jakub Jankiewicz argues that because models were trained on decades of open-source code and Creative Commons Stack Overflow answers, often without attribution, turning that knowledge into proprietary code amounts to license laundering. He adds a legal point: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human and arguably is not copyrightable, citing the monkey selfie precedent referenced by the US Copyright Office.

Since copyright law differs by country, he proposes releasing AI-generated code under open-source licenses or CC0, especially code humans barely reviewed. The post is short, but it topped 1,100 points and 600 comments.

stories.headline: A fan group pitches a three-row CyberSUV built at no added cost to Tesla, with Tesla signing its first FSD license
stories.why_read: You reposted it, and it is a creative idea at the intersection of two things Tesla fans keep asking for: new models and FSD licensing.
body: UP (@UnpluggedTesla) published Phase 3 of its proposal, titled Saving the Line: A CyberSUV at No Added Cost to Tesla. The group says 82% of its survey respondents want a three-row CyberSUV and that the production line that could build it is about to be dismantled.

Its pitch is that the vehicle could be kept alive while Tesla keeps the intellectual property, signs its first FSD license and earns on every vehicle. It is a fan proposal, not a Tesla plan, but the replies show how much appetite there is for a larger Cyber-styled family vehicle.

stories.headline: Dream praises Tesla FSD, JerryRigEverything calls out years of overstated promises, and the debate stays surprisingly civil
stories.why_read: A fair-minded exchange about what FSD is today, useful context for every Robotaxi headline.
body: Content creator Dream described his experience with Tesla's Full Self-Driving since 2021 as often more reliable than human drivers, though still needing supervision, according to a summary of posts on X. Tech reviewer JerryRigEverything praised its life-saving potential but criticized Tesla for implying Level 5 autonomy when FSD is an SAE Level 2 system that requires constant attention.

Users praised Jerry's measured tone even when they disagreed, and many shared their own accounts of strong routine performance with interventions needed in edge cases. It is a good snapshot of where public opinion sits as Tesla keeps pushing FSD marketing.

stories.headline: Starlink brings every rural municipal school in Rondonópolis, Brazil, online, and expands in Dominican Republic classrooms
stories.why_read: For the kindness corner of your pinned post: tablets, digital libraries and kids in places broadband never reached.
body: Elon Musk highlighted Starlink's role in education as every rural municipal school in Rondonópolis, Brazil, came online this month, according to a summary of posts on X. In the Dominican Republic, Starlink serves 1,608 students at two campuses, and officials met with SpaceX about expanding to more remote schools.

Officials are also eyeing Grok Tutor for personalized lessons under teacher supervision. Photos show children using tablets in newly connected classrooms, a quiet human counterpoint to a loud weekend of rocket records.
